source.version: Published journal version: Australasian Journal of Educational Technology (2026), 42(2), 39-59; DOI 10.14742/ajet.10564. Journal identification and citation appear on PDF pp. 1 and 21 (printed pp. 39 and 59). No revision/version date is stated in the article.
source.title_on_document: Exploring the impact of ChatGPT on college students’ mathematical creativity: A quasi-experimental study

supplement.holds: No supplementary material or appendix is mentioned or included in the supplied PDF. The creativity means, SDs, t statistics and d values are in Table 5, and ANCOVA F statistics and partial eta-squared values are in the main Results text (PDF pp. 11-12, printed pp. 49-50).

paper_design_summary: College students volunteering at Yangzhou University were assigned to solve open-ended mathematical creativity tasks with ChatGPT and structured prompting guidance or with traditional tools and no assistance; the Methods explicitly states random assignment in a supervised classroom, despite the quasi-experimental label in the title (PDF pp. 1, 4-7; printed pp. 39, 42-45). The analyzed sample comprised 124 students: 60 in the ChatGPT group and 64 in the control group (PDF p. 5, Figure 1, and p. 7, Participants/Table 2; printed pp. 43, 45). Two scorers classified and scored the participants’ solutions for flexibility, fluency and originality, with each indicator summed across four tasks produced while the assigned assistance was available; the post-task questionnaire measured self-evaluation and perceptions (PDF pp. 8-11, printed pp. 46-49).

assignment.what_was_assigned: Individual students were assigned to task resolution with ChatGPT or task resolution without ChatGPT. The procedure reports random assignment but does not specify how the sequence was generated. The title and abstract instead describe the study as quasi-experimental.
assignment.quote: All students were randomly assigned to either the experimental group (task resolution with ChatGPT) or the control group (task resolution without ChatGPT).
assignment.locator: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 42), Methods, Procedure; conflicting label on PDF p. 1 (printed p. 39), title and abstract.

arms.name: Experimental (task resolution with ChatGPT)
arms.description: Students used ChatGPT on personal computers, with introductory guidance and structured prompts for generating, checking and refining solutions (PDF pp. 5-7, printed pp. 43-45, Procedure, Figure 2 and Table 1). Analyzed group size is shown in Figure 1 (PDF p. 5, printed p. 43).

arms.name: Control (task resolution without ChatGPT)
arms.description: Students solved the same tasks using traditional tools, such as paper and pencil, without support or external prompts (PDF p. 5, printed p. 43, Figure 1 and Procedure). Analyzed group size is shown in Figure 1.

participants.exclusions: Students who withdrew were not included in the analysis and their questionnaires were not collected; the authors say none of the collected questionnaires were excluded. Initial assignment totals, withdrawal counts, allocation of withdrawals and reasons are not reported. The reported final sample and arm sizes are coded as analyzed, not randomized (PDF p. 4, printed p. 42, Procedure; PDF p. 5, printed p. 43, Figure 1; PDF p. 7, printed p. 45, Participants/Table 2).
participants.who: College students at Yangzhou University recruited across majors by counsellors, volunteering for course credits. The authors report no specific mathematics background and similar prior mathematics-course performance. Sessions were supervised in a quiet classroom, with participants working in separate areas (PDF p. 4, printed p. 42, Procedure; PDF p. 7, printed p. 45, Participants).
participants.quote: a sensitivity analysis was conducted based on the sample size (n = 124)
participants.locator: PDF p. 7 (printed p. 45), Participants and Table 2; PDF p. 5 (printed p. 43), Figure 1, for N = 60 and N = 64; PDF p. 4 (printed p. 42), Procedure, for recruitment, country and withdrawals.

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT; GPT-4o is shown by the model label in Figure 2 (PDF p. 6, printed p. 44). Exact model snapshot is not stated.
ai_tool.how_used: Students interacted with ChatGPT through a browser, supplied prompts, received proposed solutions and feedback, and could request modifications or provide documents. Structured example prompts, heuristic mentoring, task reminders and critical-thinking guidance were provided; the intervention therefore combines interactive chat and prompting support. Interaction logs were recorded. Students could not switch models (PDF pp. 5-7, printed pp. 43-45, Procedure, Figure 2 and Table 1).

task.description: Four open-ended mathematical creativity tasks: generate distinct 2 cm² shapes on a 4 × 4 point grid; propose ways to measure dispersion of five marbles; identify properties of water and its interface in a tilted rectangular prism; and find shared properties among eight geometries. A separate number-pyramid creativity task served as the pre-intervention baseline. These are multiple-solution tasks, not a single-answer accuracy test (PDF p. 8, printed p. 46, Measures/Table 3; PDF p. 9, printed p. 47, Figure 3).
task.duration: The experiment lasted 72 minutes (SD = 7) in the experimental group and 60 minutes (SD = 5) in the control group. These are the reported experiment durations, not a stated common time limit (PDF p. 5, printed p. 43, Procedure).

outcomes.name: MCT flexibility
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of distinct correct answer categories within each participant’s solutions. This is within-person flexibility, not diversity across participants. Two scorers independently marked solutions as correct or incorrect and classified the correct solutions; discrepancies were resolved to agreement. Each participant’s score for this indicator was summed across the four mathematical creativity tasks. The analysis unit is the participant, not a solution or a rating. Scorers’ qualifications and blinding are not stated. PDF pp. 9-10 (printed pp. 47-48), Mathematical creativity scoring. The independent-sample t test and ANCOVA adjusting for prior ChatGPT experience are analyses of the same outcome, not separate outcomes (PDF p. 8, printed p. 46, Data analysis).

contrasts.reported: Experimental M = 15.12, SD = 3.71; Control M = 12.50, SD = 3.49; t(122) = 4.05, d = 0.73, p = 0.000 (as printed in Table 5). Analyzed arm sizes: Experimental N = 60 and Control N = 64 (Figure 1). ANCOVA controlling for prior ChatGPT experience: F(1,121) = 16.60, η²p = 0.12, p < 0.001. The Table 5 note and Data analysis section state that p values were adjusted using the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 11 (printed p. 49), Table 5 row 4 and Results, H1a-c; PDF p. 5 (printed p. 43), Figure 1, for arm sizes; PDF p. 8 (printed p. 46), Data analysis.

outcomes.name: MCT originality
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Frequency-based rarity score for human-coded answer categories. The paper calculates the proportion of each answer category among total responses and assigns 3, 2, and 1 points for the printed frequency bands "0, 1%; 1%, 2%; or 2%, 3%", respectively. For Task 1 it describes summing the category originality scores within a participant, counting each category only once. Coded category_count because the score derives from manually classified category frequencies; it is not an embedding or model-generated score. The reference pool for the category frequencies is not explicitly identified by condition. Two scorers independently marked solutions as correct or incorrect and classified the correct solutions; discrepancies were resolved to agreement. Each participant’s score for this indicator was summed across the four mathematical creativity tasks. The analysis unit is the participant, not a solution or a rating. Scorers’ qualifications and blinding are not stated. PDF pp. 9-10 (printed pp. 47-48), Mathematical creativity scoring. The independent-sample t test and ANCOVA adjusting for prior ChatGPT experience are analyses of the same outcome, not separate outcomes (PDF p. 8, printed p. 46, Data analysis).

ANCOVA controlling for prior ChatGPT experience: F(1,121) = 5.44, η²p = 0.04, p = 0.021. The Table 5 note and Data analysis section state that p values were adjusted using the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction.

sample_overlap.shares_participants_with: Not stated; the paper does not identify participants as reused from another study.
sample_overlap.locator: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 42), Methods, Procedure, describes recruitment for this experiment. The Liu et al. (2025) item in the reference list is a meta-analysis, not an identified source of these participants (PDF p. 19, printed p. 57, References).

company_involvement.description: No company involvement is reported. Author affiliations are Yangzhou University departments; the Funding section lists research and education grants/programmes. ChatGPT is the intervention tool.
company_involvement.locator: PDF p. 1 (printed p. 39), author affiliations; PDF p. 18 (printed p. 56), Funding.

eligibility.reason: Methods explicitly states random assignment of individual students to ChatGPT-assisted versus unassisted task resolution (PDF p. 4, printed p. 42, Procedure); the controlled classroom session supports lab_rct coding. There were 124 analyzed people, with 60 in the experimental group and 64 in the control group (PDF p. 7, printed p. 45, Participants; PDF p. 5, printed p. 43, Figure 1). Human-coded flexibility, fluency and originality scores were derived from the students’ actual solutions to open-ended tasks (PDF pp. 8-10, printed pp. 46-48, Measures and Mathematical creativity scoring; PDF p. 11, printed p. 49, Table 5). The conflicting quasi-experimental label is flagged for audit; classification follows the explicit allocation statement. AI was available during production of the scored solutions, so these are with_ai outcomes (PDF pp. 5-7, printed pp. 43-45, Procedure/Figures 1-2/Table 1).

one_line_finding: Among 124 analyzed students, the ChatGPT group scored higher than the unassisted group on mathematical flexibility (d = 0.73), fluency (d = 0.66) and originality (d = 0.42) (PDF p. 11, printed p. 49, Table 5; sample size: PDF p. 7, printed p. 45, Participants).
open_questions: The title and abstract call this a quasi-experiment, while Methods explicitly reports random assignment; the allocation mechanism is not described (PDF pp. 1 and 4, printed pp. 39 and 42).

How many students were initially assigned and how many withdrew from each group is not reported; the final analyzed counts should not be treated as assignment counts (PDF p. 4, printed p. 42, Procedure).

The reference pool used to determine originality-category frequencies, and whether scorers were blind to condition, are not clearly stated (PDF pp. 9-10, printed pp. 47-48, Mathematical creativity scoring).
Participant overlap with other mathematical-creativity papers cannot be confirmed from this PDF; no shared-sample statement is provided.
notes:
Screened independently as B. Locators use the one-based PDF page followed by the printed journal page. The full markdown conversion and all PDF pages were read; raster Figures 1-5 were also inspected in memory. No appendix or supplement is included or referenced. The document lists Gang Li among the authors, which the search-record author shorthand omits (PDF p. 1, printed p. 39). 
Outcome inventory checked before coding: Table 5 (PDF p. 11, printed p. 49) reports baseline creativity; self-efficacy without ChatGPT and with ChatGPT; MCT flexibility, fluency and originality; self-evaluation of flexibility, fluency and originality; bias indices for flexibility, fluency and originality; interest; difficulty; effort; and perceived usefulness of ChatGPT. Table 6 (PDF p. 13, printed p. 51) gives correlations among these measures and prior ChatGPT experience. Figure 4 shows self-efficacy and Figure 5 shows interest, difficulty and effort (PDF pp. 12 and 14, printed pp. 50 and 52). Figures 1-3 show the procedure, interface and tasks; Tables 1-4 contain prompting guidance, demographics, the baseline task and solution-classification rules (PDF pp. 5-10, printed pp. 43-48). 
Only the three MCT performance indicators scored on solutions produced during the assigned condition are coded as eligible output outcomes. Baseline creativity was measured before the intervention, so it does not answer an AI-effect question. Self-efficacy, self-evaluation, interest, difficulty, effort and tool usefulness are self-reports; bias indices assess calibration of self-evaluation against performance rather than creativity of the output. The post-test in Figure 1 is a metacognitive questionnaire, not a new unassisted creativity task. No after_ai or across_people outcome is reported. Originality uses rarity to score individual solutions, not an across-person diversity contrast. 
The four task scores are summed separately for each creativity indicator; no post-intervention overall-creativity composite or task-specific treatment contrasts are reported (PDF p. 10, printed p. 48, scoring; PDF p. 11, printed p. 49, Table 5). The paper states hypotheses for these indicators but does not explicitly designate a primary outcome or mention preregistration, so primary is not_stated. Participant-level means/SDs, printed d values and adjusted-analysis statistics are transcribed; no effect size, standard error or confidence interval was calculated. Table 5 prints p = 0.000 for flexibility and fluency; those strings are retained as printed. No numerical confidence intervals or standard errors for the creativity contrasts are given. 
Interpretation limits: the AI group also received structured prompting guidance and spent longer in the experiment. The paper acknowledges that a human-prompt condition would help isolate AI effects and that time could affect the number and development of solutions (PDF p. 14, printed p. 52, Discussion; PDF p. 17, printed p. 55, Limitations). The source also gives inconsistent descriptions of external browser access: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 43) says searches were allowed but unused, whereas PDF p. 6 (printed p. 44) says external resources were not permitted. Both accounts describe ChatGPT as the aid actually used. No public data or code URL is provided.
